items.content: The AI Office is seeking input from experts on embedded evaluations of general-purpose AI (GPAI) models with systemic risk. iStock Photo Getty Images + The AI Office is hosting an online workshop in January 2027 focusing on embedded evaluations as a means of assessing systemic risks stemming from general-purpose AI (GPAI) models . 'Embedded evaluation' refers to an approach in which qualified independent evaluators – who are external to the GPAI model provider – are given employee-like access to the provider’s internal models, systems, staff and documentation to assess systemic risks over an extended period (examples: AI Evaluator Forum’s public letter and white paper by GovAI ). This workshop will bring together relevant AI safety experts and AI Office staff, possibly drawing on perspectives from GPAI model providers to exchange views on the current state of the art in conducting embedded evaluations. Worskhop's focus areas This workshop will focus on these aspects (this is a non-exaustive list and the questions are illustrative): Qualifications Which qualification criteria would be relevant for embedded evaluators, in addition to the baseline qualification criteria discussed in the AI Office’s workshop on the requirements for qualified independent external evaluators of GPAI models ? How could evaluators’ non-public work (e.g. work covered by confidentiality agreements) be taken into account when assessing their expertise and track record? What role – if any – could public, embedded-specific qualification tiers play? Who could grade the evaluators (e.g. a regulator such as the AI Office)? Access What access could be appropriate for embedded evaluators, depending on the scope of the assessment? For example: internal-only models, training data, internal deployment logs, monitoring systems, incident records and additional information such as pre-notice about new training methods used. What duration and frequency could be appropriate (e.g. continuous, fixed-term or periodic)? How could the scope of the assessment be defined/expanded during the evaluation, if necessary? How can related disputes be resolved? Transparency What could be reasonable publication rights for embedded evaluators, (e.g. regarding engagement terms, access granted and refused, methods, findings and evidence)? On what grounds might a provider redact or delay publication and for how long? How could reports handle redacted material (e.g. by indicating what was redacted and whether it affects the conclusions)? The workshop may also discuss other aspects of embedded evaluations. For instance: their scope (e.g. which systemic risks are best assessed through embedded evaluations? Which systems would be unlikely to be assessed adequately?) additional independence safeguards that the engagement of embedded evaluators may call for (e.g. cooling-off periods and rotation of individual evaluators). The workshop aims to solicit expert opinions on relevant aspects of state-of-the-art embedded evaluations. How to participate? The AI Office invites proposals on possible approaches to conduct embedded evaluations. The proposals will be the base for selecting participants. The AI Office will share a consolidated document based on the submissions, which will inform the workshop discussions. Selected participants will be able to comment on this document ahead of the workshop. We particularly welcome expressions of interest and submissions from those who have conducted embedded evaluations, plan to do so shortly, or have published proposals involving embedded evaluations. The proposals submitted do not need to cover all the points listed above and may go beyond them. Apollo Research’s Principles for Embedded Evaluations and the AI Evaluator Forum’s Minimum Conditions for Embedding Evaluators illustrate what a proposal could cover. You can express your interest and submit your proposal until 9 December 2026 . Participants selection and the start of the comment round is also foreseen for December 2026. Fill the form to express your interest Eligibility and selection Applicants will be selected on the basis of the quality and relevance of their submitted proposals and of the following criteria, particularly as they relate to embedded evaluations: Demonstrated experience in conducting high-quality evaluations of GPAI models and their systemic risks (e.g. in-depth evaluations of capabilities, propensities, risks, safety mitigation effectiveness, including red teaming, uplift studies, white-box evaluations) and/or A quality track record of AI governance thought leadership with a focus on evaluations of systemic risks (e.g. prominent white papers). Individuals and organisations that have engaged in embedded evaluations and wish to participate may submit an expression of interest without a proposal. In that case, they should indicate their prior experience with embedded evaluations. An expression of interest without a proposal is also permissible for individuals or organisations that belong to the AI Office’s Network of Evaluators and can demonstrate recent or ongoing relevant work on embedded evaluations. They should likewise indicate this. (The AI Office considers that an individual or organisation belongs to the Network of Evaluators if they consented to this when taking part in any of the workshops on 13 December 2024 , 28 April 2025 or 15 July 2026 .) Disclaimer This call is issued by the AI Office to gather input for a workshop on embedded evaluations. The content and questions set out here are intended to prompt discussion. They do not represent an official position of the AI Office or the European Commission, and they are not guidance on the application of AI Act. This call is without prejudice to that regulation and to any acts or guidelines adopted under it. Proposals and comments received reflect the views of their authors only. The workshop is not intended to cover the expertise, competence, independence or any other requirements of the AI Act's Scientific Panel (as established under Article 68(2) of the AI Act) or the independent experts that the Commission may appoint to conduct evaluations on the basis of Article 92(2) of the AI Act. Last update 27 November 2026 Print as PDF

items.title: Building on Nemotron 3.5 Parse: Open Data, Fine-Tuning, and Faster Inference
items.summary: Back to Articles Building on Nemotron 3.5 Parse: Open Data, Fine-Tuning, and Faster Inference Enterprise + Article Published November 26, 2026 Upvote 26 +20 Ryan Chesler emelryan Follow nvidia Marek Wawrzos mwawrzos Follow nvidia Steve Han steve-nvidia Follow nvidia We recently released NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Parse , a compact document model that turns page images into structured data for retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) and agents. Now we’re building on that release with synthetic training datasets, a fine-tuning recipe, and a DFlash2 speculator for faster inference . We’re also sharing how we trained Parse 3.5: first teaching document understanding through supervised fine-tuning, then using reinforcement learning to improve accuracy, consistency, and reliable completion. items.content: Back to Articles Building on Nemotron 3.5 Parse: Open Data, Fine-Tuning, and Faster Inference Enterprise + Article Published November 26, 2026 Upvote 26 +20 Ryan Chesler emelryan Follow nvidia Marek Wawrzos mwawrzos Follow nvidia Steve Han steve-nvidia Follow nvidia We recently released NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Parse , a compact document model that turns page images into structured data for retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) and agents. Now we’re building on that release with synthetic training datasets, a fine-tuning recipe, and a DFlash2 speculator for faster inference . We’re also sharing how we trained Parse 3.5: first teaching document understanding through supervised fine-tuning, then using reinforcement learning to improve accuracy, consistency, and reliable completion. What Parse 3.5 produces Parse extracts content from pages of documents into reading order, assigns content classes such as headings, paragraphs, tables, and charts, and returns bounding boxes that locate the content. Tables and charts become structured records that can power downstream document processing applications. Figure 1. Actual model output from a synthetic operations brief, showing the connection between the page and its structured representation. This latest version of Parse significantly extends its ability to read charts and tables, especially in more difficult and ambiguous cases. For example, bar charts or other plots that do not have any marked numeric values. The model is able to infer values by looking at the axes and height of the bar to derive these. items.content: Algorithms and theory Google’s mission presents many exciting algorithmic and optimization challenges across different product areas including Search, Ads, Social, and Google Infrastructure. These include optimizing internal systems such as scheduling the machines that power the numerous computations done each day, as well as optimizations that affect core products and users, from online allocation of ads to page-views to automatic management of ad campaigns, and from clustering large-scale graphs to finding best paths in transportation networks. Other than employing new algorithmic ideas to impact millions of users, Google researchers contribute to the state-of-the-art research in these areas by publishing in top conferences and journals. Recent Publications See More The Visibility VC-Dimension of Simple Polygons is Six Dror Aiger Sariel Har-Peled 2027 Preview Preview abstract We prove that no simple polygon P ⊂ R 2 contains a visibility-shattered set of seven points, establishing that the maximum visibility VC-dimension over all simple polygons is six. Combined with Valtr’s lower bound [Val98], this resolves the visibility VC-dimension problem for simple polygons, improving the upper bound of 23 due to Valtr [Val98] and 14 due to Gilbers and Klein [GK14] to the exact value 6. We also exhibit an explicit 968-vertex simple polygon with rational vertex coordinates that shatters six points in strictly convex position, confirming maxP VC-dim(P) = maxP VC-dimconvex(P) = 6. Our proof combines a general-position perturbation, a structural decomposition of the convex hull of a shattered seven-point set into a contiguous block of certified front vertices and non-certified hull vertices, an extended polygonenclosure calculus, and a sound chirotope reduction whose geometric soundness implications are machine-checked in Lean 4 and independently verified via Z3 real-arithmetic proofs and dual CDCL SAT solvers. View details Hadwiger’s Covering Conjecture in Three Dimensions Dror Aiger Sariel Har-Peled Goran Žužić 2027 Preview Preview abstract Let K in R^3 be an arbitrary convex body, that is, a compact convex subset of R^3 with nonempty interior. We prove unconditionally that K can be covered by eight smaller positive homothetic copies of itself: there exist a scalar lambda in (0, 1) and translation vectors v_1, ..., v_8 in R^3 such that K is contained in the union of (lambda K + v_i) for i = 1, ..., 8. This resolves Hadwiger's covering conjecture in three dimensions. The proof works in Boltyanski's equivalent boundary illumination formulation and is completely self-contained. Parallelepipeds are covered directly by eight translates of (2/3)K. For any convex body K that is not a parallelepiped, we place its centrally symmetric halved difference body S = (1/2)(K - K) in John's position (B^3 subseteq S) and show that the spherical average of its support function satisfies 8 int_{S^2} h_S d sigma_tilde < 12, with equality only for orthogonal cubes. Using outer polyhedral approximations together with Cauchy's planar perimeter formula, the full spherical measure of directions not parallel to any boundary segment of K, and lower semicontinuity of curve variation, we find a unit vector w_* in S^2 whose shadow boundary Sigma(K, w_*) on K itself is a continuous closed curve of S-length strictly less than 12. Splitting Sigma(K, w_*) into six contiguous arcs of S-length strictly less than 2 and applying Helly's theorem in R^3 illuminates each arc with one direction, while +-w_* illuminate the remainder of partial K. The proof was discovered using an experimental harness on top of Gemini 4 Carbon and formally verified in Lean 4. View details Depth-CoT Tradeoffs in Transformers: A Look at Path Following Clayton Sanford Matus Telgarsky Justin D. Li 2027 Preview Preview abstract Modern transformers have been scaled up in size, data, training-time compute, and more recently test-time compute based on Chain-of-Thought (CoT), but the consequences of trading off these parameters are unknown. We construct explicit tradeoffs between two of these aspects: the number of layers in a transformer and the number of CoT tokens. Our first result is general: with mild assumptions and a single-token prompt, for any integer k, a transformer using soft attention and SwiGLU MLP layers with L layers and n CoT tokens can be converted to a transformer with at most ckL layers and ⌈n/k⌉ CoT tokens, and vice versa, although with an increase to the size of other parameters. We then a multi-token prompt path following task, finding that additional preprocessing from the multi-token prompt changes the depth-CoT relationship in this case. We construct an attention-only network with L layers and 2^(L−2) heads that can traverse 2^(L−1) − 1 edges along a path with a single CoT token, demonstrating at least an exponential relationship between increases in depth and reductions in the number of CoT tokens needed to traverse the entire path. This relationship for the path following task holds empirically as well, as demonstrated by training networks with up to 5 layers, with the tradeoff between depth and the maximum number of edge traversals in a single CoT token exactly matching our theoretical constructions. View details Geo-Contextual AI Concierge: Minimizing Internal Support Friction Through Proactive Knowledge Synthesis Neeraj Choudhary Dónal Doyle Technical Report (2026) Preview Preview abstract In large-scale distributed enterprises, traditional Knowledge Management (KM) systems face a critical failure mode: static documentation cannot keep pace with evolving operational realities and regional nuances. This "knowledge latency" forces employees out of self-service workflows and into costly support ticketing queues. This paper introduces SENTINEL, a geo-contextual AI framework designed to shift enterprise support from reactive retrieval to proactive interception. The architecture employs a novel dual-engine system integrated into an omni-present interface. The first engine utilizes Large Language Models (LLMs) to conduct pre-emptive, historical case-grounded audits of documentation, generating a "Contextual Density" score that identifies friction zones. The second engine is an autonomous Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) agent that surfaces in-situ via a location-intelligent assistant window, resolving queries in real-time. By functioning as a strategic "defensive barrier" at the point of origin, SENTINEL demonstrates how a proactive AI assistant can drive high-fidelity, in-situ case deflection. View details Rational Transductors Mehryar Mohri ICML 2026 Preview Preview abstract Standard Transformers excel at semantic modeling but struggle with rigid sequential logic and state tracking, fundamentally limited to AC0 complexity without intermediate chain-of- thought. In this work, we introduce Rational Transductors, a dual-stream architecture that augments the Transformer with a linear, matrix-valued recurrence derived from Weighted Finite Automata (WFA). By injecting rational state information into the attention mechanism via a Deep Rational Injection scheme, our framework strictly generalizes the expressive power of Transformers to capture all Regular Languages and NC1-complete problems (such as Parity and Modular Counting) while preserving O(log T) parallel training efficiency. View details Marginalized Bundle Adjustment: Multi-View Camera Pose from Monocular Depth Estimates Shengjie Zhu Ahmed Abdelkader Mark Matthews Xiaoming Liu Vincent Chu International Conference on 3D Vision (2026) Preview Preview abstract Structure-from-Motion (SfM) is a classical 3D vision task for recovering camera parameters and scene geometry from multi-view images. Recent advances in deep learning enable accurate monocular depth estimation (MDE) that infers structure from a single image without depending on camera motion. But integrating MDE into SfM remains challenging. Unlike classical triangulated sparse pointclouds, MDE produces dense depthmaps with significantly higher error variance. Inspired by modern RANSAC estimators, we propose a Marginalized Bundle Adjustment (MBA) to accommodate MDE error variance with its density. With MBA, we show that MDE depthmaps are sufficiently accurate to support SoTA or competitive results in Structure-from-Motion and camera relocalization. Our benchmark demonstrates consistent remarkable results from two-view, few-frames small multiview, to thousands-frames large multiview system. Our method highlights the significant potential of MDE on multi-view 3D vision tasks. Recent advances in deep learning enable accurate monocular depth estimation (MDE) that infers structure from a single image without depending on camera motion. But integrating MDE into SfM remains challenging. Unlike classical triangulated sparse pointclouds, MDE produces dense depthmaps with significantly higher error variance. Inspired by modern RANSAC estimators, we propose a Marginalized Bundle Adjustment (MBA) to accommodate MDE error variance with its density. With MBA, we show that MDE depthmaps are sufficiently accurate to support SoTA or competitive results in Structure-from-Motion and camera relocalization. Our benchmark demonstrates consistent remarkable results from two-view, few-frames small multiview, to thousands-frames large multiview system. Our method highlights the significant potential of MDE on multi-view 3D vision tasks. items.content: Back to Articles Introducing harness adapters: adapt your favorite model to your harness to improve performance and cost Published November 20, 2026 Update on GitHub Upvote 166 +160 Younes B ybelkada Follow ben burtenshaw burtenshaw Follow Nathan Habib SaylorTwift Follow Lysandre lysandre Follow Amine Dirhoussi aminediroHF Follow Adithya S K AdithyaSK Follow shaun smith evalstate Follow Sergio Paniego sergiopaniego Follow Joel Niklaus joelniklaus Follow Lewis Tunstall lewtun Follow Combining RL on a custom task distribution with your favorite agent harness yields more accurate and efficient models for that target harness and task distribution. Models are not fully optimized for all harnesses and the tasks you’re doing. Instead, they target general performance. So when you combine a model and harness, you’re leaving performance and efficiency on the table for the stuff you’re actually doing. With RL, you can train a custom harness adapter that squeezes everything out of your model for your harness and task combination. Take Qwen3.8-27B, its Terminal-Bench 2.1 score with the pi harness is 39% which uses on average 2.9K tokens per task. If we freeze those weights and add a custom RL-trained LoRA adapter we can get 55% pass@1, with average token usage of 1.5K. Most of this is down to the model reasoning less, calling less tools, and performing better first time. Our earlier work ( multi-harness RL , harness adapters ) showed that RL on your own task distribution, inside your own harness, gives a more accurate and more efficient model. Those experiments covered data-analysis and code-building tasks. Here we wanted to push this further by exploring whether the result holds at 27B, on harder real-world software engineering tasks, across three harnesses: Pi, OpenCode and Hermes Agent. And most of all, share a fully reusable recipe, so you can reproduce this on your own task, harness, model combinations. TL;DR We trained one LoRA adapter for Qwen3.8-27B per agent harness (pi, Hermes Agent, OpenCode), with RL inside the harness itself. Datasets, training and agent rollouts all happen on the Hub in Jobs using TRL's AsyncGRPOTrainer , OpenEnv and harbor. Each harness adapter beats the base model under its own harness on both benchmarks, for both performance and efficiency. The three LoRAs are also merged into a single super adapter that runs unchanged under pi, Hermes Agent and OpenCode. All artifacts (adapters, GGUFs, RL tasks, safeagents plugin) can be browsed through this Hugging Face collection . Table of Contents Training inside agent harnesses Generating custom RL tasks on Hugging Face Testing the filters with short training runs AsyncGRPOTrainer for more efficient GRPO training Training setup Super-adapter: merging all adapters into one Final results Open question: What did the model really learn to do? Closing words and future directions Training inside agent harnesses We leverage the Harbor integration in OpenEnv and TRL’s OpenEnv guide to train the model inside the harnesses we chose for the final training. We have built ready-to-use docker images for all our RL tasks that come with the target harnesses already pre-installed inside. In our final docker images, we use Pi 1.5.2 , OpenCode 2.2.7 and Hermes Agent v0.22.6 . The diagram below from the aforementioned blogpost explains well the entire protocol: Most RL frameworks train a re-implementation of the agent loop: the agent is written against the framework's own interface, such as verl's AgentLoop , SkyRL-Gym environments, rLLM 's agent and environment classes, slime 's custom rollout functions, or ART 's client inside your own Python agent. Here the harness runs exactly as it ships, and the trainer learns from the exact tokens it produced, recorded by a proxy between the harness and vLLM. Recent work moves in the same direction: Agent Lightning v1.0 keeps the deploy-time harness in the loop through a proxy ("harnessed agentic RL"), and SkyRL's Harbor integration trains on Harbor trials, converting their chat histories into tokens for the trainer. Generating custom RL tasks on Hugging Face For this recipe we created a custom dataset for agentic coding with the Hub, OpenEnv, and Repo2RLEnv . We combined together task retrieval of existing RL envs, task generation with Repo2RLEnv, task validation with OpenEnv, and sampling into a single data pipeline. This gave us the highest quality set of validated and relevant tasks to improve Qwen3.8-27B on agentic coding. In this section, we’ll walk through how we built it, so you can try it out on your own domains. RL training needs tasks the agent can attempt, a verifier that scores each attempt, and evidence that the verifier is right. A verifier that accepts wrong answers teaches the wrong behavior. A task that is already feasible will not teach the model anything. This section describes how we built the task set from three sources: two on the Hugging Face Hub and a third generated with Tasksmith, a pipeline in Repo2RLEnv. Every task passes an eligibility screen with openenv validate , and the same difficulty check against the base model, Qwen3.8-27B. Three sources Each task uses the Harbor format, which Terminal-Bench 2.1 also uses. A broad search of the Hub for Harbor environments returned about 59,000 tasks, but they included duplicates, evaluation sets and tasks marked as not for training. We filtered down to just two Hub sources built for training and generated a third set ourselves: SWE-smith ( Python , Go ) injects bugs into real Python and Go repositories, with an LLM rewrite or a mutation such as a flipped operator. The tests that catch each bug become the task's tests. It adds volume. SWE-Gym, packaged as Harbor tasks in TaskTrove , turns real GitHub issues and their merged fixes into tasks. It adds real-world bugs. Tasksmith generates tasks from merged pull requests. An LLM agent writes the instruction and tests, and Tasksmith checks the result: the reference and a valid alternative must pass, while the unfixed code and a known-wrong solution must fail. We used Tasksmith to target gaps. We mapped the skills that our target benchmarks test (Terminal-Bench 2.1, the hard subset of SWE-bench Pro, and DeepSWE), then chose pull requests that exercise them, such as HTTP streaming, filesystem operations and serialization. From 30 merged pull requests, Tasksmith produced 24 tasks in 10 Python repositories that passed its checks, 17 of them on a second run. Its checks do not replace ours, so these tasks go through the same pipeline as the rest. Validation with openenv validate A metadata screen runs first. It keeps tasks from training splits with permissive licenses. It drops duplicates, tasks marked as not for training, the 253 tasks in our target benchmarks, and any task from a repository those benchmarks use. We then ran the semantic checks from openenv validate on every task in fresh trials: The reference solution earns the maximum reward ( semantic.oracle_max ). Doing nothing scores clearly lower ( semantic.floor_gap ). No canary scores more than doing nothing ( semantic.canary_floor ). A replay of the reference gives the same reward ( runtime.episode_determinism ). Each trial ran as its own Hugging Face Job, which let us validate dozens of tasks at once. openenv validate offers the same option for any Harbor task: openenv validate path/to/task --sandbox hf-sandbox 858 of 1,127 Hub candidates passed. Wrong-answer controls caught defects, including a Tasksmith task that accepted an incomplete implementation and a Terminal-Bench 2.1 verifier (regex-log) that accepted known-wrong answers. Most failures were infrastructure problems, such as images that did not start. Failed tasks stay in a rejected split with the failing check recorded. Difficulty check with the base model A valid task can still teach nothing. GRPO (group relative policy optimization) scores each attempt against the other attempts at the same task, so a task where every attempt passes, or every attempt fails, gives no learning signal. Before training, Qwen3.8-27B attempted each task 4 times, or 8 times for a stratified sample of six tasks per repository. Of 442 scored tasks, Qwen3.8-27B solved 151 every time and 120 never. The 171 tasks it solved only sometimes form the qualified set. The figure below shows how the scores pile up at both ends and how they differ by source. The model solves most Go tasks every time, fails every attempt on more than a third of the SWE-smith Python tasks, and lands in the middle on 73% of the SWE-Gym tasks. Qwen3.8-27B results on 442 scored tasks. Green marks the qualified tasks, which the model solves on some attempts but not all. This example shows how we filtered and validated 1,127 tasks to 278 which we included directly in the final dataset. The pipeline then took the remaining 522 rejected tasks, repaired and complexified them with Tasksmith and repeated validation. Testing the filters with short training runs The pipeline applies two filters: validation removes broken tasks, and the difficulty check keeps tasks the base model solves only sometimes. This section tests whether those filters change what the model learns. We trained four short runs of up to 50 steps, each on tasks from a different stage of the pipeline, and compared them with the base model on Terminal-Bench 2.1. Each run trains Qwen3.8-27B with LoRA and GRPO, using TRL's AsyncGRPOTrainer , on 32 tasks. All four use the same agent harness (OpenCode with up to 48 model calls), the same settings and one 8×H200 Hugging Face Job, and the reward is the verifier's pass or fail. The task sets differ in how they were filtered: Unvalidated : 24 accepted tasks plus 8 that failed validation. Validated : 32 accepted tasks, chosen without regard to difficulty. Unqualified : 32 accepted tasks that the base model always or never solves. Qualified : 32 accepted tasks that the base model solves on some attempts. The figure below shows how the tasks impacted model learning. The table lists each run's steps and the checkpoint we evaluate. The chart tracks training reward across subsets of tasks with differing validation status. The dataset harness-hub/agentic-coding-envs holds 871 tasks from 35 repositories. Hub tasks are capped at 40 per repository, so no single project dominates. The table below shows what each source contributes. The dataset has two views: every accepted task, and the qualified subset for GRPO training. Rejected attempts stay in a separate config. Source Task type Tasks Qualified SWE-smith Injected bugs in Python and Go 717 144 SWE-Gym (TaskTrove) Real GitHub issues 130 27 Tasksmith Generated from merged pull requests 24 22 Total 871 171 AsyncGRPOTrainer for more efficient GRPO training We leveraged the stable version of AsyncGRPOTrainer from TRL, with the main advantage of the trainer being that it does not wait until all rollouts are completed before moving to the next training optimization step. For more detailed reading on the trainer and its building blocks, please refer to the AsyncGRPO blogpost . Training setup To obtain our final harness adapters, we trained LoRA adapters on top of Qwen/Qwen3.8-27B using TRL's AsyncGRPOTrainer . The adapters were attached to the model using the all-linear flag. To maximize the training efficiency, thinking mode was turned off during rollout stages, and we evaluated our final adapter with and without thinking for broader comparison. The final reward function consists of the verifier's correctness, combined with a small tool-efficiency bonus (0.1, derived from early experiments from the previous iteration of harness adapters which showed that 0.1 worked best). We performed a small LR sweep on 50 steps using Termgrade environments (1e-5, 5e-5 and 1e-4) and noticed that 1e-5 barely moved training correctness (from 0.52 to 0.50), 1e-4 collapsed the rollouts instead of improving them (turns per rollout moved from 18 to 6, with entropy rising), and only 5e-5 clearly improved (from 0.49 to 0.60 by step 40). Longer 5e-5 runs then showed signs of instability (collapsing rollout lengths, rising entropy), so we settled on 2e-5 for the final runs. Training infrastructure Each harness adapter was trained using NVIDIA 2xB200 GPUs, with one GPU allocated for the vLLM server and the other allocated for the training process. We first performed some stress testing to maximize the amount of RL tasks that can be trained within a single optimization step. For that, we ‘maxed out’ the --token-budget argument from AsyncGRPOTrainer to its limit for the setup that we had. The chart below shows the evolution of the number of groups per step for each harness (in blue: Pi, green: OpenCode and orange: Hermes). As the model gets better and better during training, it is able to fit more and more groups during each training step, which diversifies the signals that the model gets at each optimization step. Final mixture The final data mixture consists of 750 tasks from harness-adapters RL environments and 300 tasks from termgrade . In order to maximize the diversity of the sampled tasks during training, we have slightly customized the data sampling strategy, which will be explained below: Before training, the tasks are put in a fixed order that interleaves them by family (i.e., their repository for our generated RL environments. For Termgrade, we just sorted them by name since each task is considered as its own family), so every training step mixes as many repositories as possible while following the distribution of the mixture. safeagents in the loop We also plug the safeagents tool, in order to block any misbehavior from the model during training. The final plugin (which consists of the regex and pattern rules specific to the RL tasks and test path) is hosted in harness-hub/qwen-safeagents-plugin and can be used out of the box using the latest version of safeagents in case anyone wants to reproduce the training setup. The number of blocked tools from safeagents decreases consistently during training, which indicates that the model gets ‘safer and safer’ after each optimization step. Below is a diagram of the safeagents blocked calls per 1000 tool calls, by training step, for each harness adapter. Super-adapter: merging all adapters into one Merging models often combines their capabilities while keeping most of what each one could do. Once the three harness adapters were trained, we asked two questions. Does merging them cost accuracy? And can a single "super-adapter" be accurate and efficient under every harness? We started by comparing the weight updates of the three adapters, layer by layer. The cosine similarity between any two of them is about 0.01–0.02: each adapter pushed the model in a nearly orthogonal direction during training. That's the best case for merging, since the updates barely interfere. We concatenate the three LoRA adapters along the rank dimension (PEFT's combination_type="cat" ). The merged adapter has rank 96 (3 × 32) and applies exactly w · (ΔW_pi + ΔW_hermes + ΔW_opencode). Prior work on merging ( task arithmetic , TIES , KnOTS ) finds that scaling each update below 1 works best, so we compared three weights on all 89 Terminal-Bench 2.1 tasks, under each harness, with the step-120 adapters: ⅓ (the average): each harness keeps only a third of its own update. ½: each update at half strength. 1 (the plain sum): every update applied in full. Weight pi hermes opencode All three harnesses Tool calls per task base model 39.1% 46.0% 44.8% 43.3% 49.2 ⅓ (average) 49.4% 51.2% 47.1% 49.2% 35.6 ½ 48.8% 53.5% 55.2% 52.5% 25.9 1 (sum) 40.2% 62.8% 47.1% 50.0% 13.4 The plain sum over-applies the updates. The agents become very short (13 tool calls per task, against 49 for the base model), and while Hermes peaks at 62.8%, pi falls back to the base model's level. The average dilutes each harness's own update. ½ gives the best balance, so we built the final super-adapter from the released checkpoints (pi step 160, hermes step 160, opencode step 150) at weight ½. Adapter merging evaluation results Under each harness, on the tasks every run graded (50–51 on SWE-bench Pro, 82–85 on Terminal-Bench 2.1), one attempt per task (in parentheses, the efficiency gain with respect to the base model): Harness Benchmark Qwen3.8-27B Qwen3.8-27B-<harness>-adapted Qwen3.8-27B-super-adapter Qwen3.8-27B , thinking Qwen3.8-27B-super-adapter , thinking pi SWE-bench Pro (hard 51) 40.0% 64.0% (−60%) 46.0% (−73%) 74.0% 74.0% (−48%) hermes SWE-bench Pro (hard 51) 29.4% 43.1% (−56%) 47.1% (−60%) 45.1% 60.8% (−36%) opencode SWE-bench Pro (hard 51) 35.3% 51.0% (−72%) 45.1% (−63%) 47.1% 66.7% (−31%) pi Terminal-Bench 2.1 40.0% 56.5% (−56%) 48.2% (−56%) 52.9% 57.6% (−25%) hermes Terminal-Bench 2.1 44.7% 58.8% (−70%) 55.3% (−53%) 58.8% 63.5% (−19%) opencode Terminal-Bench 2.1 47.6% 52.4% (−53%) 52.4% (−68%) 54.9% 58.5% (−22%) "Thinking" is the chat template's thinking mode at its default effort (xhigh). The specialists were trained and served with thinking off. With thinking off, the super-adapter improves on the base model on all six harness–benchmark pairs (mean pass@1 39.5% → 49.0%; 71 tasks newly solved vs 34 lost, p < 0.001). Despite not being trained at all with thinking on, it's the strongest model we evaluated with thinking mode. Against the base model thinking at the same effort, it wins on five of six pairs and ties the sixth (mean 55.5% → 63.5%; 67 newly solved vs 37 lost, p = 0.004). The largest gains are on SWE-bench Pro: +16 points under hermes and +20 under opencode. Under pi on SWE-bench Pro, where thinking alone already reaches 74%, it ties. Use the specialist harness adapters when thinking off. Each harness's own adapter is ahead on four of six pairs, by the most under pi (64.0% vs 46.0% on SWE-bench Pro, 56.5% vs 48.2% on Terminal-Bench). Splitting one model across three harnesses costs pi the most of its gain. If you only use one harness and keep thinking off, take its specialist. The super adapter is also much more efficient. On the tasks both the base model and the super-adapter solve, with thinking off, it makes 53–73% fewer tool calls and generates 44–60% fewer tokens per task, with fewer tool calls on 111 of 130 tasks. With thinking on, it still cuts tool calls by 31–48% and tokens by 24–43% on SWE-bench Pro. On Terminal-Bench, tool calls drop by 19–25% and token counts stay about the same. The ½ weight was chosen on Terminal-Bench 2.1 with the step-120 adapters, so the Terminal-Bench numbers are slightly optimistic; SWE-bench Pro played no part in the choice. Full paired results are in the super-adapter's model card . Final results This section reports what happened during training, then how the adapters score on held-out benchmarks inside and outside their own harnesses. Training results Training ran for a cumulative total of 598 steps, with a total of 78,114 samples trained, which consists exactly of 167M trained tokens. During training, we see a clear signal that the model learns to solve tasks in fewer and fewer steps, with no clear sign of saturation. Despite having some clear increasing trend sometimes, training correctness seems to overall stay flat. This can be explained by the fact that the model meets new tasks during training, but the number of groups that fit in a step’s token budget more than doubles as trajectories get shorter. The accuracy gains show up on the held-out benchmarks in the section below. On the other hand, safeagents was able to block multiple suspicious attempts. Across the three training runs, a total of 1.3M tool calls have been checked, and a total of 647 tool calls have been blocked. Evaluation results This section covers the evaluation setup, the in-harness results, transfer across harnesses, and an out-of-distribution check. Evaluation setup We evaluate each adapter inside the harness it was trained in, on two agentic coding benchmarks: all 89 tasks of Terminal-Bench 2.1 (1 hour and 100 agent steps per task) and the 51 hardest tasks of SWE-bench Pro (2 hours and 100 agent steps). We cap the maximum number of tokens per task to be 131072. We do not tune the agent settings and use the default setup for all harnesses. For example, Pi automatically applies context compaction, while OpenCode and Hermes don't, which mainly affects the SWE-bench Pro results due to rapid context overflow. Therefore you cannot compare the results across different harnesses (using Pi does not necessarily lead to better results than Hermes or OpenCode), but it is fair to compare results within the same harness and draw conclusions. Every rollout runs through the same Harbor and OpenEnv stack as training, in HF sandboxes, with one attempt per task at temperature 0.8 and thinking off. Each LoRA checkpoint is merged into the base weights and served alone with vLLM on a single GPU, at the same concurrency as the base model's eval. For all the evaluation benchmarks, we report the pass@1 as well as the number of tool calls, total turns, for all tasks and for solved tasks. For openness, all model trajectories for final evaluations are pushed in this public bucket: harness-hub/harness-adapters-trajectories . Final evaluation results All three specialist adapters beat the base model under their own harness, on both benchmarks. On SWE-bench Pro (hard 51), pi goes from 39.2% to 64.7% (+25.5 points: 15 tasks newly solved vs 2 lost, p = 0.002), hermes from 29.4% to 43.1%, and opencode from 35.3% to 51.0%. On the full Terminal-Bench 2.1, pi gains +16.3 points (16 vs 2, p = 0.001) and hermes +14.1 (19 vs 7, p = 0.03). Opencode gains +6.0 overall, and +13.6 on the 66 tasks that played no part in choosing its checkpoint (12 vs 3, p = 0.035). The adapters also solve tasks much more efficiently: on the tasks both they and the base model solve, they make 56–72% fewer tool calls per task on SWE-bench Pro and 53–70% fewer on Terminal-Bench 2.1. The single super-adapter beats the base model under all three harnesses too (+6 to +18 points on SWE-bench Pro, +5 to +10 on Terminal-Bench 2.1), with just as large a cut in tool calls (53–73%). It keeps less of each specialist's gain with thinking off, most under pi, but with thinking on it beats the base model thinking at the same effort on five of six harness–benchmark pairs (see the super-adapter section ). Each model card has the full paired results. Does the efficiency and performance ability transfer across harnesses? To answer this question, we also evaluated the pi harness adapter under Hermes Agent and OpenCode. Under OpenCode it matches OpenCode's own specialist on Terminal-Bench 2.1 (44.8% → 54.0%, against 46.4% → 52.4%). Under Hermes it keeps about two-thirds of the specialist's gain (46.3% → 56.1%, against 44.7% → 58.8%), with the same ~45% cut in tool calls in both. Therefore it seems that the newly learned capabilities are transferred across harnesses. Evaluation on out-of-distribution tasks and setup What happens if we evaluate in out-of-distribution tasks, outside the harnesses the adapters have been trained with? We ran all five models on 300 AutomationBench tasks which consists of business-automation workflows evaluations, with AutomationBench's own agent loop instead of Pi, Hermes or OpenCode. This way, we can cross check two different questions: can the model solve problems outside SWE-related tasks? What happens when the model is being put outside the harness it has been trained with? Results show that the adapters stay close to the base model. Pi and OpenCode are slightly ahead (27.0% and 25.3% pass@1 against 23.0%), the merged adapter is level (23.7%), and Hermes is a few points behind (17.7%). The differences are within noise, except perhaps Hermes, therefore RL inside the harnesses neither transfers clearly to this very different setting nor breaks the model on it. Model pass@1 (all assertions met) vs base Partial credit (share of assertions met) vs base base 23.0% 62.2% pi 160 27.0% +4.0 66.2% +4.0 opencode 150

Datasets, training and agent rollouts all happen on the Hub in Jobs using TRL's AsyncGRPOTrainer , OpenEnv and harbor. Each harness adapter beats the base model under its own harness on both benchmarks, for both performance and efficiency. The three LoRAs are also merged into a single super adapter that runs unchanged under pi, Hermes Agent and OpenCode. All artifacts (adapters, GGUFs, RL tasks, safeagents plugin) can be browsed through this Hugging Face collection . Table of Contents Training inside agent harnesses Generating custom RL tasks on Hugging Face Testing the filters with short training runs AsyncGRPOTrainer for more efficient GRPO training Training setup Super-adapter: merging all adapters into one Final results Open question: What did the model really learn to do? Closing words and future directions Training inside agent harnesses We leverage the Harbor integration in OpenEnv and TRL’s OpenEnv guide to train the model inside the harnesses we chose for the final training. We have built ready-to-use docker images for all our RL tasks that come with the target harnesses already pre-installed inside. In our final docker images, we use Pi 1.5.2 , OpenCode 2.2.7 and Hermes Agent v0.22.6 . The diagram below from the aforementioned blogpost explains well the entire protocol: Most RL frameworks train a re-implementation of the agent loop: the agent is written against the framework's own interface, such as verl's AgentLoop , SkyRL-Gym environments, rLLM 's agent and environment classes, slime 's custom rollout functions, or ART 's client inside your own Python agent. Here the harness runs exactly as it ships, and the trainer learns from the exact tokens it produced, recorded by a proxy between the harness and vLLM. Recent work moves in the same direction: Agent Lightning v1.0 keeps the deploy-time harness in the loop through a proxy ("harnessed agentic RL"), and SkyRL's Harbor integration trains on Harbor trials, converting their chat histories into tokens for the trainer. Generating custom RL tasks on Hugging Face For this recipe we created a custom dataset for agentic coding with the Hub, OpenEnv, and Repo2RLEnv . We combined together task retrieval of existing RL envs, task generation with Repo2RLEnv, task validation with OpenEnv, and sampling into a single data pipeline. This gave us the highest quality set of validated and relevant tasks to improve Qwen3.8-27B on agentic coding. In this section, we’ll walk through how we built it, so you can try it out on your own domains. RL training needs tasks the agent can attempt, a verifier that scores each attempt, and evidence that the verifier is right. A verifier that accepts wrong answers teaches the wrong behavior. A task that is already feasible will not teach the model anything. This section describes how we built the task set from three sources: two on the Hugging Face Hub and a third generated with Tasksmith, a pipeline in Repo2RLEnv. Every task passes an eligibility screen with openenv validate , and the same difficulty check against the base model, Qwen3.8-27B. Three sources Each task uses the Harbor format, which Terminal-Bench 2.1 also uses. A broad search of the Hub for Harbor environments returned about 59,000 tasks, but they included duplicates, evaluation sets and tasks marked as not for training. We filtered down to just two Hub sources built for training and generated a third set ourselves: SWE-smith ( Python , Go ) injects bugs into real Python and Go repositories, with an LLM rewrite or a mutation such as a flipped operator. The tests that catch each bug become the task's tests. It adds volume. SWE-Gym, packaged as Harbor tasks in TaskTrove , turns real GitHub issues and their merged fixes into tasks. It adds real-world bugs. Tasksmith generates tasks from merged pull requests. An LLM agent writes the instruction and tests, and Tasksmith checks the result: the reference and a valid alternative must pass, while the unfixed code and a known-wrong solution must fail. We used Tasksmith to target gaps. We mapped the skills that our target benchmarks test (Terminal-Bench 2.1, the hard subset of SWE-bench Pro, and DeepSWE), then chose pull requests that exercise them, such as HTTP streaming, filesystem operations and serialization. From 30 merged pull requests, Tasksmith produced 24 tasks in 10 Python repositories that passed its checks, 17 of them on a second run. Its checks do not replace ours, so these tasks go through the same pipeline as the rest. Validation with openenv validate A metadata screen runs first. It keeps tasks from training splits with permissive licenses. It drops duplicates, tasks marked as not for training, the 253 tasks in our target benchmarks, and any task from a repository those benchmarks use. We then ran the semantic checks from openenv validate on every task in fresh trials: The reference solution earns the maximum reward ( semantic.oracle_max ). Doing nothing scores clearly lower ( semantic.floor_gap ). No canary scores more than doing nothing ( semantic.canary_floor ). A replay of the reference gives the same reward ( runtime.episode_determinism ). Each trial ran as its own Hugging Face Job, which let us validate dozens of tasks at once. openenv validate offers the same option for any Harbor task: openenv validate path/to/task --sandbox hf-sandbox 858 of 1,127 Hub candidates passed. Wrong-answer controls caught defects, including a Tasksmith task that accepted an incomplete implementation and a Terminal-Bench 2.1 verifier (regex-log) that accepted known-wrong answers. Most failures were infrastructure problems, such as images that did not start. Failed tasks stay in a rejected split with the failing check recorded. Difficulty check with the base model A valid task can still teach nothing. GRPO (group relative policy optimization) scores each attempt against the other attempts at the same task, so a task where every attempt passes, or every attempt fails, gives no learning signal. Before training, Qwen3.8-27B attempted each task 4 times, or 8 times for a stratified sample of six tasks per repository. Of 442 scored tasks, Qwen3.8-27B solved 151 every time and 120 never. The 171 tasks it solved only sometimes form the qualified set. The figure below shows how the scores pile up at both ends and how they differ by source. The model solves most Go tasks every time, fails every attempt on more than a third of the SWE-smith Python tasks, and lands in the middle on 73% of the SWE-Gym tasks. Qwen3.8-27B results on 442 scored tasks. Green marks the qualified tasks, which the model solves on some attempts but not all. This example shows how we filtered and validated 1,127 tasks to 278 which we included directly in the final dataset. The pipeline then took the remaining 522 rejected tasks, repaired and complexified them with Tasksmith and repeated validation. Testing the filters with short training runs The pipeline applies two filters: validation removes broken tasks, and the difficulty check keeps tasks the base model solves only sometimes. This section tests whether those filters change what the model learns. We trained four short runs of up to 50 steps, each on tasks from a different stage of the pipeline, and compared them with the base model on Terminal-Bench 2.1. Each run trains Qwen3.8-27B with LoRA and GRPO, using TRL's AsyncGRPOTrainer , on 32 tasks. All four use the same agent harness (OpenCode with up to 48 model calls), the same settings and one 8×H200 Hugging Face Job, and the reward is the verifier's pass or fail. The task sets differ in how they were filtered: Unvalidated : 24 accepted tasks plus 8 that failed validation. Validated : 32 accepted tasks, chosen without regard to difficulty. Unqualified : 32 accepted tasks that the base model always or never solves. Qualified : 32 accepted tasks that the base model solves on some attempts. The figure below shows how the tasks impacted model learning. The table lists each run's steps and the checkpoint we evaluate. The chart tracks training reward across subsets of tasks with differing validation status. The dataset harness-hub/agentic-coding-envs holds 871 tasks from 35 repositories. Hub tasks are capped at 40 per repository, so no single project dominates. The table below shows what each source contributes. The dataset has two views: every accepted task, and the qualified subset for GRPO training. Rejected attempts stay in a separate config. Source Task type Tasks Qualified SWE-smith Injected bugs in Python and Go 717 144 SWE-Gym (TaskTrove) Real GitHub issues 130 27 Tasksmith Generated from merged pull requests 24 22 Total 871 171 AsyncGRPOTrainer for more efficient GRPO training We leveraged the stable version of AsyncGRPOTrainer from TRL, with the main advantage of the trainer being that it does not wait until all rollouts are completed before moving to the next training optimization step. For more detailed reading on the trainer and its building blocks, please refer to the AsyncGRPO blogpost . Training setup To obtain our final harness adapters, we trained LoRA adapters on top of Qwen/Qwen3.8-27B using TRL's AsyncGRPOTrainer . The adapters were attached to the model using the all-linear flag. To maximize the training efficiency, thinking mode was turned off during rollout stages, and we evaluated our final adapter with and without thinking for broader comparison. The final reward function consists of the verifier's correctness, combined with a small tool-efficiency bonus (0.1, derived from early experiments from the previous iteration of harness adapters which showed that 0.1 worked best). We performed a small LR sweep on 50 steps using Termgrade environments (1e-5, 5e-5 and 1e-4) and noticed that 1e-5 barely moved training correctness (from 0.52 to 0.50), 1e-4 collapsed the rollouts instead of improving them (turns per rollout moved from 18 to 6, with entropy rising), and only 5e-5 clearly improved (from 0.49 to 0.60 by step 40). Longer 5e-5 runs then showed signs of instability (collapsing rollout lengths, rising entropy), so we settled on 2e-5 for the final runs. Training infrastructure Each harness adapter was trained using NVIDIA 2xB200 GPUs, with one GPU allocated for the vLLM server and the other allocated for the training process. We first performed some stress testing to maximize the amount of RL tasks that can be trained within a single optimization step. For that, we ‘maxed out’ the --token-budget argument from AsyncGRPOTrainer to its limit for the setup that we had. The chart below shows the evolution of the number of groups per step for each harness (in blue: Pi, green: OpenCode and orange: Hermes). As the model gets better and better during training, it is able to fit more and more groups during each training step, which diversifies the signals that the model gets at each optimization step. Final mixture The final data mixture consists of 750 tasks from harness-adapters RL environments and 300 tasks from termgrade . In order to maximize the diversity of the sampled tasks during training, we have slightly customized the data sampling strategy, which will be explained below: Before training, the tasks are put in a fixed order that interleaves them by family (i.e., their repository for our generated RL environments. For Termgrade, we just sorted them by name since each task is considered as its own family), so every training step mixes as many repositories as possible while following the distribution of the mixture. safeagents in the loop We also plug the safeagents tool, in order to block any misbehavior from the model during training. The final plugin (which consists of the regex and pattern rules specific to the RL tasks and test path) is hosted in harness-hub/qwen-safeagents-plugin and can be used out of the box using the latest version of safeagents in case anyone wants to reproduce the training setup. The number of blocked tools from safeagents decreases consistently during training, which indicates that the model gets ‘safer and safer’ after each optimization step. Below is a diagram of the safeagents blocked calls per 1000 tool calls, by training step, for each harness adapter. Super-adapter: merging all adapters into one Merging models often combines their capabilities while keeping most of what each one could do. Once the three harness adapters were trained, we asked two questions. Does merging them cost accuracy? And can a single "super-adapter" be accurate and efficient under every harness? We started by comparing the weight updates of the three adapters, layer by layer. The cosine similarity between any two of them is about 0.01–0.02: each adapter pushed the model in a nearly orthogonal direction during training. That's the best case for merging, since the updates barely interfere. We concatenate the three LoRA adapters along the rank dimension (PEFT's combination_type="cat" ). The merged adapter has rank 96 (3 × 32) and applies exactly w · (ΔW_pi + ΔW_hermes + ΔW_opencode). Prior work on merging ( task arithmetic , TIES , KnOTS ) finds that scaling each update below 1 works best, so we compared three weights on all 89 Terminal-Bench 2.1 tasks, under each harness, with the step-120 adapters: ⅓ (the average): each harness keeps only a third of its own update. ½: each update at half strength. 1 (the plain sum): every update applied in full. Weight pi hermes opencode All three harnesses Tool calls per task base model 39.1% 46.0% 44.8% 43.3% 49.2 ⅓ (average) 49.4% 51.2% 47.1% 49.2% 35.6 ½ 48.8% 53.5% 55.2% 52.5% 25.9 1 (sum) 40.2% 62.8% 47.1% 50.0% 13.4 The plain sum over-applies the updates. The agents become very short (13 tool calls per task, against 49 for the base model), and while Hermes peaks at 62.8%, pi falls back to the base model's level. The average dilutes each harness's own update. ½ gives the best balance, so we built the final super-adapter from the released checkpoints (pi step 160, hermes step 160, opencode step 150) at weight ½. Adapter merging evaluation results Under each harness, on the tasks every run graded (50–51 on SWE-bench Pro, 82–85 on Terminal-Bench 2.1), one attempt per task (in parentheses, the efficiency gain with respect to the base model): Harness Benchmark Qwen3.8-27B Qwen3.8-27B-<harness>-adapted Qwen3.8-27B-super-adapter Qwen3.8-27B , thinking Qwen3.8-27B-super-adapter , thinking pi SWE-bench Pro (hard 51) 40.0% 64.0% (−60%) 46.0% (−73%) 74.0% 74.0% (−48%) hermes SWE-bench Pro (hard 51) 29.4% 43.1% (−56%) 47.1% (−60%) 45.1% 60.8% (−36%) opencode SWE-bench Pro (hard 51) 35.3% 51.0% (−72%) 45.1% (−63%) 47.1% 66.7% (−31%) pi Terminal-Bench 2.1 40.0% 56.5% (−56%) 48.2% (−56%) 52.9% 57.6% (−25%) hermes Terminal-Bench 2.1 44.7% 58.8% (−70%) 55.3% (−53%) 58.8% 63.5% (−19%) opencode Terminal-Bench 2.1 47.6% 52.4% (−53%) 52.4% (−68%) 54.9% 58.5% (−22%) "Thinking" is the chat template's thinking mode at its default effort (xhigh). The specialists were trained and served with thinking off. With thinking off, the super-adapter improves on the base model on all six harness–benchmark pairs (mean pass@1 39.5% → 49.0%; 71 tasks newly solved vs 34 lost, p < 0.001). Despite not being trained at all with thinking on, it's the strongest model we evaluated with thinking mode. Against the base model thinking at the same effort, it wins on five of six pairs and ties the sixth (mean 55.5% → 63.5%; 67 newly solved vs 37 lost, p = 0.004). The largest gains are on SWE-bench Pro: +16 points under hermes and +20 under opencode. Under pi on SWE-bench Pro, where thinking alone already reaches 74%, it ties. Use the specialist harness adapters when thinking off. Each harness's own adapter is ahead on four of six pairs, by the most under pi (64.0% vs 46.0% on SWE-bench Pro, 56.5% vs 48.2% on Terminal-Bench). Splitting one model across three harnesses costs pi the most of its gain. If you only use one harness and keep thinking off, take its specialist. The super adapter is also much more efficient. On the tasks both the base model and the super-adapter solve, with thinking off, it makes 53–73% fewer tool calls and generates 44–60% fewer tokens per task, with fewer tool calls on 111 of 130 tasks. With thinking on, it still cuts tool calls by 31–48% and tokens by 24–43% on SWE-bench Pro. On Terminal-Bench, tool calls drop by 19–25% and token counts stay about the same. The ½ weight was chosen on Terminal-Bench 2.1 with the step-120 adapters, so the Terminal-Bench numbers are slightly optimistic; SWE-bench Pro played no part in the choice. Full paired results are in the super-adapter's model card . Final results This section reports what happened during training, then how the adapters score on held-out benchmarks inside and outside their own harnesses. Training results Training ran for a cumulative total of 598 steps, with a total of 78,114 samples trained, which consists exactly of 167M trained tokens. During training, we see a clear signal that the model learns to solve tasks in fewer and fewer steps, with no clear sign of saturation. Despite having some clear increasing trend sometimes, training correctness seems to overall stay flat. This can be explained by the fact that the model meets new tasks during training, but the number of groups that fit in a step’s token budget more than doubles as trajectories get shorter. The accuracy gains show up on the held-out benchmarks in the section below. On the other hand, safeagents was able to block multiple suspicious attempts. Across the three training runs, a total of 1.3M tool calls have been checked, and a total of 647 tool calls have been blocked. Evaluation results This section covers the evaluation setup, the in-harness results, transfer across harnesses, and an out-of-distribution check. Evaluation setup We evaluate each adapter inside the harness it was trained in, on two agentic coding benchmarks: all 89 tasks of Terminal-Bench 2.1 (1 hour and 100 agent steps per task) and the 51 hardest tasks of SWE-bench Pro (2 hours and 100 agent steps). We cap the maximum number of tokens per task to be 131072. We do not tune the agent settings and use the default setup for all harnesses. For example, Pi automatically applies context compaction, while OpenCode and Hermes don't, which mainly affects the SWE-bench Pro results due to rapid context overflow. Therefore you cannot compare the results across different harnesses (using Pi does not necessarily lead to better results than Hermes or OpenCode), but it is fair to compare results within the same harness and draw conclusions. Every rollout runs through the same Harbor and OpenEnv stack as training, in HF sandboxes, with one attempt per task at temperature 0.8 and thinking off. Each LoRA checkpoint is merged into the base weights and served alone with vLLM on a single GPU, at the same concurrency as the base model's eval. For all the evaluation benchmarks, we report the pass@1 as well as the number of tool calls, total turns, for all tasks and for solved tasks. For openness, all model trajectories for final evaluations are pushed in this public bucket: harness-hub/harness-adapters-trajectories . Final evaluation results All three specialist adapters beat the base model under their own harness, on both benchmarks. On SWE-bench Pro (hard 51), pi goes from 39.2% to 64.7% (+25.5 points: 15 tasks newly solved vs 2 lost, p = 0.002), hermes from 29.4% to 43.1%, and opencode from 35.3% to 51.0%. On the full Terminal-Bench 2.1, pi gains +16.3 points (16 vs 2, p = 0.001) and hermes +14.1 (19 vs 7, p = 0.03). Opencode gains +6.0 overall, and +13.6 on the 66 tasks that played no part in choosing its checkpoint (12 vs 3, p = 0.035). The adapters also solve tasks much more efficiently: on the tasks both they and the base model solve, they make 56–72% fewer tool calls per task on SWE-bench Pro and 53–70% fewer on Terminal-Bench 2.1. The single super-adapter beats the base model under all three harnesses too (+6 to +18 points on SWE-bench Pro, +5 to +10 on Terminal-Bench 2.1), with just as large a cut in tool calls (53–73%). It keeps less of each specialist's gain with thinking off, most under pi, but with thinking on it beats the base model thinking at the same effort on five of six harness–benchmark pairs (see the super-adapter section ). Each model card has the full paired results. Does the efficiency and performance ability transfer across harnesses? To answer this question, we also evaluated the pi harness adapter under Hermes Agent and OpenCode. Under OpenCode it matches OpenCode's own specialist on Terminal-Bench 2.1 (44.8% → 54.0%, against 46.4% → 52.4%). Under Hermes it keeps about two-thirds of the specialist's gain (46.3% → 56.1%, against 44.7% → 58.8%), with the same ~45% cut in tool calls in both. Therefore it seems that the newly learned capabilities are transferred across harnesses. Evaluation on out-of-distribution tasks and setup What happens if we evaluate in out-of-distribution tasks, outside the harnesses the adapters have been trained with? We ran all five models on 300 AutomationBench tasks which consists of business-automation workflows evaluations, with AutomationBench's own agent loop instead of Pi, Hermes or OpenCode. This way, we can cross check two different questions: can the model solve problems outside SWE-related tasks? What happens when the model is being put outside the harness it has been trained with? Results show that the adapters stay close to the base model. Pi and OpenCode are slightly ahead (27.0% and 25.3% pass@1 against 23.0%), the merged adapter is level (23.7%), and Hermes is a few points behind (17.7%). The differences are within noise, except perhaps Hermes, therefore RL inside the harnesses neither transfers clearly to this very different setting nor breaks the model on it. Model pass@1 (all assertions met) vs base Partial credit (share of assertions met) vs base base 23.0% 62.2% pi 160 27.0% +4.0 66.2% +4.0 opencode 150

items.content: Back to Articles How to build and maintain an agentic evaluation Published November 23, 2026 Update on GitHub Upvote 70 +64 Avijit Ghosh evijit Follow ben burtenshaw burtenshaw Follow Irene Solaiman irenesolaiman Follow Overview AI evaluations help shape which systems people build, adopt, and trust. An evaluation gives a system tasks, checks its answers or actions, and produces a score. Building and maintaining a useful evaluation therefore takes real work: defining tasks that reflect domain expertise, scoring them reliably, and checking that the results support the claims made. When methods, code, and data stay private, that work is harder for others to scrutinize or build on. Open source offers a means to build stronger, more frequently updated, and more comparable evaluations and the infrastructure around them. Existing tasks, environments, and tools give builders a starting point, so their effort can go to domain expertise and validation. Sharing how an evaluation was built, including what went wrong, lets others find errors, improve it, and reuse it. The Hugging Face hub is the home for AI evaluation: we host around 3500 eval leaderboards and have seen about a 16X growth in eval datasets on the hub in the past year , to about 17000 datasets. In recent months, we have also incorporated support for agentic abstractions that are relevant to evaluation. For example, Traces that store an agent’s work in an easily reviewable and sharable way; Benchmarks that highlight datasets used to evaluate models with leaderboards; and Environments that show datasets used as agentic RL or evaluation environments. This guide covers four things: Three eras of evaluation (section 1). Evaluations moved from checking answers, to checking what an agent did, to checking what a team of agents produces. Each step adds software that can change the score. The steps in an agentic evaluation (section 2). We follow one task through eight steps, from the claim to the reported score. The full walkthrough, with commands, is in Appendix A . When a benchmark is wrong (section 3). Errors in tasks and graders are common. We look at how they are found and corrected. What to open strategically and why (section 4). A table sets out, component by component, what to share and what can stay protected. In the research community, AI evaluation terminology is notoriously inconsistent . The glossary at the end defines each term we use and notes the other names you may come across. 1. Introduction: how evaluation design has changed AI evaluation design has evolved in three forms as language models have become more capable and able to perform more complex work: question answer, agentic, and teams or swarms. Question-answer benchmarks such as MMLU (2020) and GPQA (2023) measure knowledge and reasoning through the answers models produce. As models became capable of planning and using tools, agentic benchmarks such as SWE-bench and WebArena expanded the scope to resolving software issues and completing tasks on websites. These tasks require evaluation setups that account for the environment in which the system operates and the changes it makes. Lately, research on multi-agent systems has started to add another dimension: how agents coordinate and what they accomplish together. This includes decentralized swarms , teams managed by an orchestrator , and specialized agents collaborating on scientific work . Figure 1 shows a rough timeline of these three eras of evaluations. Figure 1. Three types of language model evals. Question-and-answer benchmarks check a response against a key. Agentic benchmarks check what an agent changed in an environment. Team and swarm benchmarks score what a group of agents produced. We’ll focus on agentic evaluations in this article for two reasons. First, they are becoming increasingly the most prominent type in model release announcements due to high user and enterprise interest in agentic deployment. Second, they offer a useful starting point for understanding how evaluation design affects model performance. Team and swarm evaluations introduce further complexity through interactions between agents, which we leave outside the scope of this guide. Once an agent uses tools to complete a task, each part of the surrounding software can affect its score. For instance, in an audit of Terminal-Bench , researchers kept the model fixed and changed the agent harness. Accuracy varied by up to 29.9 percentage points. To understand differences like that, we examine the anatomy of an agentic evaluation and follow one task from the instructions the agent receives to the checks that determine whether it passed. The anatomy of an agentic evaluation Figure 2. The different components of an agentic evaluation. There are various parts to an agentic evaluation. A task gives the agent its instruction. The agent harness wraps the model and its tools, letting it work inside a pinned environment. During one rollout, the agent attempts the task from start to finish: it may run several commands, inspect their output, and try again before it stops. The evaluation harness runs several rollouts for each task. When a rollout ends, the verifier grades the environment's final state. Each rollout also leaves a trace, and traces and scores together become part of the final published evidence. Each part can be published, inspected, and reused separately. Why benchmark release decisions matter Demand for independent evaluation is growing. Policymakers, enterprises, and researchers want evaluations they can verify, and today they mostly cannot: 98.2% of model-benchmark scores are reported by only one party , and researchers have argued that in-house evaluation is not enough . At the same time, more benchmarks are holding back test items to reduce contamination: questions or solutions entering training data, so scores may reflect prior exposure. Artificial Analysis says 60% of its Intelligence Index v5 , announced in October 2026, rests on evaluations with private test sets or held-out answers. Google DeepMind recently piloted double-blind evaluations , where a secure enclave hides an outside evaluator's test prompts from the model provider and the model's weights from the evaluator. While that can reduce contamination, privacy by itself does not guarantee quality, and withholding supporting materials can make expert review harder. We argue that builders can and should still share infrastructure, grading methods, and evidence about task design. Scrutiny depends on giving others a way to question the measurement and correct mistakes, including controlled review where public release is unsuitable. 2. Building an eval: what to reuse, adapt, and validate With the anatomy in place, we now build one agentic evaluation for a real use case: an agent that analyzes measurements for a physics lab. Rather than starting from scratch, we adapt an open task, so most of our effort goes into domain expertise and validation. We work through eight steps: define the claim , find a task , run it unchanged , adapt it , check the evaluation , read the traces , report the score , and compare models . We then take stock of what we reused. The full walkthrough is in Appendix A . Figure 3 maps the steps and what each produced in our example. Figure 3. The eight steps of building an agentic evaluation. The left panel highlights each step in turn, and the right panel shows what it involved in our example. Yellow steps work on the evaluation itself, and orange steps run models and read the results. Method Claim. Consider a physics lab that wants an agent to fit peaks in a Raman spectrum. A Raman spectrum is a measurement whose peaks reveal properties of a material, here graphene. The agent's job is ordinary coding: read the data file, fit a curve to each peak, and save the results (Figure 5 in Appendix A). For the purposes of this article, our claim is deliberately narrow: fit the specified peaks, calculate the requested D-to-G ratio (the intensity of one peak relative to another, which can indicate defects in the material; we also call it the defect ratio), and save accurate results consistently. Reviewing a whole lab report would need additional skills and evidence. Starting task and baseline. We reused the Harbor task format and Terminal-Bench's raman-fitting task. Harbor is an open source evaluation harness, and Terminal-Bench is an open benchmark of tasks that an agent completes in a terminal. We first ran the task's reference solution, which passed, and then ran the original task three times with Terminus-2 , a terminal agent harness, and gpt-oss-120b , an open-weight model from OpenAI. Harbor ran inside an HF Job, each rollout used its own HF Sandbox, and Inference Providers supplied the model responses. Reusing the runner and task format let us concentrate on the physics, grading, and review. Only the agent harness needed no new work. Every other component needed checking or new work, which we list part by part at the end of Appendix A . Adaptation. We built raman-lab : eight synthetic spectra with known parameters and varied noise and defect levels. The adaptation fits three peaks instead of two and reports a defect ratio. We used an agent to help generate the spectra, reviewed them by hand, and wrote new instructions, reference fits, and output checks. The new instructions state the units and parameter definitions that the original left implicit. These eight tasks are a development set, meaning tasks we use while building the evaluation; broader coverage should follow the variation in real measurements. Checks. Before executing more model runs, we tested the evaluation itself. We ran the reference solution, an agent that does nothing, and a shortcut that skips the required work. The reference solution should pass every task, and the other two should fail. Our shortcut read the height of each peak straight from the data and guessed the widths. It returned the expected defect ratio on all eight tasks without fitting the spectra, so we added checks on the fit itself. Shortcut. We also tested a shortcut to check how robust the evaluation is against cheating. Our shortcut is a short script that skips the actual fitting. It reads the tallest point of each peak straight from the data, guesses the peak widths, and divides the D height by the G height. Even so, it returned the expected defect ratio on all eight tasks, so a grader that checked only the ratio would have given it full marks. We added checks on each fitted peak, and the final verifier rejects it. Results Figure 4. What we learned by measuring different aspects while building the evaluation. (A) Testing the grader with a shortcut showed that a ratio-only check could be fooled. (B) Reading gpt-oss-120b’s traces showed that most of its failures came from stopping early. (C) Running other models showed that the tasks can be solved. Appendix A has the detailed results in Figure 7 (how gpt-oss-120b’s attempts ended), Figure 8 (all six models) and Figure 9 (when each model said it was done). Baseline. On the original task, gpt-oss-120b passed 0 of 3 rollouts. items.summary: Back to Articles Where scientists draw the line on AI agents Enterprise Article Published November 25, 2026 Upvote 9 +3 Kyle Wiggers Ai2Comms Follow allenai 📄 Tech Report Delegating research tasks to AI does not remove scientists’ responsibility for how the work is accomplished. For example, a researcher using AI to review the literature needs to check whether the system overlooks conflicting evidence or makes claims the cited papers don’t support. Someone handing off data analysis to an agentic system needs to understand which methods it used, which files it accessed, and whether the results can be successfully reproduced.
